title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
event_hint: An empirical comparison of Semantic Search (prebuilt vector-index retrieval) versus Deep Agentic Search (planner delegating exploration to an isolated subagent, a.k.a. grep-search by subagent) on the SWE-QA repo-level code-QA benchmark; Semantic search is more accurate and cheaper, while Deep Agentic search introduces a new hand-off failure class.
problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating the right code in a repository, and the choice between index-based Semantic Search and hierarchical Deep Agentic Search (used to protect the main agent from context rot / context pollution) has direct consequences for accuracy, cost, and latency. Recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) adopted Deep Agentic Search quickly, but the two paradigms had not been empirically compared for repository-level code question answering, so the debate rests largely on intuition.
mechanism: Two agent architectures are compared on SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a) across four language models. The Semantic side is a flat ReAct agent (LangChain ReAct harness) restricted to three tools: a repository-structure lookup, a retrieval tool over a vector index built once per repo (file chunking + embedding + similarity retrieval), and a file reader. The Deep Agentic side is a hierarchical Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework, default toolset: planning, a virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation). Each question runs in a fresh conversation thread with only the target repository available; all tool calls, planner steps, sub-agent actions, and token counts are recorded. Answers are graded by an LLM judge validated against an independent human panel. The authors argue the two action spaces cannot be made identical because the tool difference is intrinsic to each paradigm rather than a confound.

evidence.claim: Semantic search answers 65.2% of questions correctly versus 46.2% for Deep Agentic search (pooled across the four model conditions, matching the mean of the per-model Pass rates in Table 3). The within-model Pass-rate difference favours Semantic by 5.6pp (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 10.0pp (Gemini 2.5 Pro), 10.6pp (Qwen3-235B), and 49.6pp (Gemini 3 Flash); all four McNemar and all four Wilcoxon tests remain significant after false discovery rate correction.
evidence.value: 65.2% vs 46.2% (pooled); +5.6 to +49.6pp Semantic advantage per model
evidence.baseline: Deep Agentic search within the same model and benchmark
evidence.condition: SWE-QA benchmark, four LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B); Cliff's delta ~0.14 for the Gemini 2.5 pair, 0.24 for Qwen3-235B, 0.76 for Gemini 3 Flash (effect modest for Gemini 2.5, large only for Gemini 3 Flash)
evidence.source_locator: Abstract PDF Page 1; Table 3 and paired within-model comparison, PDF Page 15

evidence.claim: Semantic search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of Deep Agentic search. Per-model dollars-per-Pass: Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.213 vs 0.436; Gemini 2.5 Pro 1.048 vs 1.526; Gemini 3 Flash 0.179 vs 0.858; Qwen3-235B 0.012 vs 0.291.
evidence.value: $/Pass roughly 2x cheaper for Semantic across all four models
evidence.baseline: Deep Agentic search $/Pass within the same model
evidence.condition: Cost includes reasoning tokens billed at completion rate (so cost is not the simple product of the in/out token columns and list prices); token columns count prompt+completion tokens only
evidence.source_locator: Abstract PDF Page 1; Table 3, PDF Page 15

evidence.claim: A six-mechanism failure taxonomy shows Deep Agentic search did not eliminate failures but introduced a new class: the single largest share of Deep failures, 41.8%, were coordination breakdowns at the planner-to-sub-agent hand-off, and 0% for Semantic (a flat retrieval agent has no such hand-off). The association between architecture and failure mechanism is very strong: chi-square 508.8 on 5 df, Cramer's V 0.56; restricted to the five mechanisms available to both architectures the association remains large (chi-square 147.2 on 4 df, V 0.35).
evidence.value: 41.8% of Deep failures are coordination breakdowns; 0% for Semantic
evidence.baseline: Semantic-search failure distribution over the same taxonomy
evidence.condition: Coded from recorded execution traces; hand-off failures usually silent, ending in a fluent confident wrong answer
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.3 / Figure 19, PDF Page 26; restated in Abstract PDF Page 1

evidence.claim: Despite higher cost and lower accuracy, Deep Agentic search has lower median latency for three of four models: Gemini 2.5 Flash 106s vs 329s (Semantic), Gemini 2.5 Pro 152s vs 400s, Qwen3-235B 105s vs 42s (here Deep is slower), and Gemini 3 Flash 262s vs 101s (Deep slower). The latency trade-off is therefore model-dependent and does not consistently favour either paradigm.
evidence.value: Median latency per question from Table 3 (model-dependent)
evidence.baseline: Semantic search median latency within the same model
evidence.condition: Single-question fresh conversation; latency in seconds

evidence.claim: The LLM judge was validated against an independent human panel on a stratified sample of 800 answers (100 per condition): human-panel Fleiss kappa 0.81 [0.78, 0.84] (three raters, 88.5% exact agreement); human-vs-judge Cohen kappa 0.74 pooled (Semantic conditions 0.78, Deep conditions 0.69); numeric score Pearson r 0.83, Spearman rho 0.81, mean absolute difference 5.2 score points.
evidence.value: Human-vs-judge Cohen kappa 0.74; Pearson r 0.83; MAD 5.2 points
evidence.condition: 800 stratified answers; judge agreement lower on Deep conditions (MAD 6.8) than Semantic (MAD 4.1)

evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a), open-ended questions over whole Python repositories; each question answered in a fresh thread with only the target repository available. Four LLMs: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B. Two architectures: ReAct agent (LangChain) with three tools (repo-structure lookup, vector-index retrieval, file reader), vector index built once per repo via chunking+embedding; and Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework) with planning, virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation. Grading by LLM judge cross-validated against a human panel. Failure taxonomy inter-coder agreement: two authors on 400 failures, Cohen kappa 0.86 (symptom) and 0.78 (mechanism), consensus-vs-automatic coding 0.82.
limitations: Scope is read-only repository question answering over repositories that can be indexed; results do not cover code modification, patching, or SWE-Bench-style edit tasks, and the abstract explicitly restricts the conclusion to 'read-only questions over a repository that can be indexed.' The accuracy advantage is consistent in direction across all four models but modest in magnitude for the Gemini 2.5 pair (Cliff's delta ~0.14) and large only for Gemini 3 Flash; part of the large Gemini 3 Flash Pass-rate gap (49.6pp from a 30.9-point score difference) reflects the fixed Pass cutoff rather than the underlying score scale. The two architectures have non-identical action spaces (different tools), which the authors treat as intrinsic to the paradigms rather than a confound but which limits controlled attribution. Judge agreement is lower on Deep conditions (Cohen kappa 0.69, MAD 6.8) than Semantic (0.78, MAD 4.1). The coordination-breakdown failure is partly definitional because only a hierarchical agent can produce it.
project_relevance: Directly informs the agent-acceleration question of whether repository indexing truly lowers end-to-end task cost: for read-only repo QA, a prebuilt vector index is both more accurate and roughly half the cost per correct answer than delegating exploration to an isolated subagent. It also supplies the failure-mode evidence the topic asks about for tool-call delegation correctness risks, quantifying that the largest failure source of the hierarchical design (41.8%) is the planner-subagent hand-off, often producing silently wrong answers. The latency data is a genuine counterpoint (Deep is faster for some models) and means cost/accuracy and latency can diverge, so an indexing shortcut is not automatically the lowest-latency option. Applicability is bounded to read-only QA on indexable repos and should not be extrapolated to patching or editing workflows without separate evidence.
